strengths: Addresses critical gap in low-resource NLP for 1.4 billion Indian language speakers with practical resource efficiency (<$1,000 training budget on single GPU)
Comprehensive evaluation across 21 baseline models with multiple benchmarks, ablation studies, human evaluation (κ=0.85-0.87), and cross-lingual transfer analysis
Strong open-science contribution with publicly released models, tokenizers, and instruction-tuning datasets enabling reproducibility and community use
Hybrid Unigram+BPE tokenization shows consistent improvements (1-2% benchmarks, superior fertility scores) with clear morphological benefits demonstrated in Table 7
Efficient empirical results: outperforms all LLMs <3B parameters and competitive with 3-8B models while being 10-100× smaller and trained on 50-100× less data
Thorough data preprocessing pipeline (language identification, deduplication, toxicity filtering, script-specific handling) and instruction-tuning with quality guidelines (Fleiss Kappa 0.87)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: tokenization combines existing methods (Bostrom & Durrett 2020), RoPE scaling adapted from Chen et al. (2023); core contribution is engineering/domain application rather than algorithmic innovation

Fundamental data constraints significantly limit capabilities: 54.6GB (25-66B tokens) is 50-100× less than competitive models; limited domain diversity causes weak MMLU performance (often below random baseline for Tamil/Telugu), indicating knowledge gaps

Evaluation concerns: zero-shot only (no task-specific fine-tuning), 1024-token context length, weak knowledge benchmarks, and overstated claims (e.g., 'outperforms most larger models' only true for <3B models)
Instruction-tuning dataset too small (23K examples) with quality degradation from machine translation (8-13% WER); modest improvements (1-4% most languages); limited analysis of practical utility
Unexplained n-shot degradation (Table 14) where performance drops 0→25 shot, suggesting weak in-context learning ability; unclear why Telugu differs from other languages
Training convergence not verified: models trained with GPU interruptions over 42-239 hours, hyperparameter transfer robustness via μP not validated, detailed training logs omitted
Safety deficits: no safety mechanisms despite acknowledging models generate 'factually incorrect, biased, inappropriate content'; non-commercial license limits adoption compared to open alternatives
Model capability limitations: low CPU inference speeds (12-42 tokens/sec), unclear real-world deployment readiness, no task-specific application examples beyond benchmarks

strengths: Addresses critical gap in NLP for underrepresented Indian languages covering 10 languages across 5 scripts
Comprehensive and practical contribution with monolingual, bilingual, and multilingual model variants
Demonstrates efficient deployment with CPU-only inference, showing competitive performance with models 20-64x larger
Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple benchmarks (ARC, MMLU, HellaSwag, XNLI, XCOPA, etc.) and human evaluation
Novel mBharat tokenizer achieves competitive/superior fertility scores compared to LLaMa-3.1, Gemma-2, and GPT-4o
Significant resource contributions including 23k instruction-tuning datasets per language for 5 languages
Well-motivated typological grouping strategy for multilingual pretraining to avoid curse of multilinguality
Practical value through demonstration of various downstream capabilities (grammar correction, poetry, summarization, etc.)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: RoPE scaling method is straightforward (context_length / max_permissible_length) lacking mathematical formulation and theoretical justification; tokenizer combines existing BPE and Unigram techniques; missing ablation studies

Significant human evaluation limitations: only 3 of 10 languages evaluated (Bangla, Hindi, Sanskrit); missing critical details (annotator count, inter-annotator agreement, detailed guidelines); no statistical significance testing

Unfair baseline comparisons: GPT-3.5-Turbo comparisons problematic as Figures 4-5 show complete failures on Indian text, suggesting model doesn't support these languages; comparing models trained on different data/compute budgets without controls

Benchmark evaluation concerns: uses machine-translated versions of standard benchmarks (ARC, MMLU, HellaSwag) which may introduce translation artifacts; no perplexity comparisons with baselines; unexplained anomalies (performance drops in few-shot settings, Table 4)

Critical reproducibility deficits: no information on code/model release; incomplete architecture details (embedding dim, layers, heads, FFN); RoPE scaling cannot be reproduced from description; tokenizer training procedure underspecified

Data and experimental design issues: unusual 95%-5% train-val split with minimal validation data; dramatic token count imbalance across languages (26.2B-66B) not addressed; instruction dataset is heterogeneous mix (5k human, 15k Google-translated, 3k self-instruct) without quality analysis

Missing analysis depth: no explanation for extreme perplexity variation across languages (1.75 for Sanskrit vs. 16.99 for Hindi 162M); limited language transfer analysis; absent error analysis and discussion of failure modes; no evaluation of translation quality impact

Presentation and scope limitations: human-evaluated samples appear cherry-picked; no significance testing across benchmark results (many differences <2%); missing discussion of ethical considerations, data biases, and limitations; incomplete related work on position-based scaling techniques
